**Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina** (born c. 1525, [Palestrina](https://www.britannica.com/place/Praeneste), near [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome) [Italy]—died February 2, 1594, Rome) was an Italian [Renaissance](https://www.britannica.com/event/Renaissance) composer of more than 105 masses and 250 motets, a master of contrapuntal [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition).

Palestrina lived during the period of the Roman Catholic [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) and was a primary representative of the 16th-century [conservative](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/conservative) approach to [church music](https://www.britannica.com/topic/liturgical-music).

## Life

Palestrina was born in a small town where his ancestors are thought to have lived for generations, but as a child he was taken to nearby Rome. In 1537 he was one of the choirboys at the basilica of [Santa Maria Maggiore](https://www.britannica.com/place/Santa-Maria-Maggiore-church-Rome-Italy), where he also studied [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) between 1537 and 1539. In 1544 Palestrina was engaged as organist and singer in the cathedral of his native town. His duties included playing the organ, helping with the choir, and teaching music. His pay was that of a [canon](https://www.britannica.com/art/canon-music) and would have been received in money and kind. His [prowess](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/prowess) at the church there attracted the attention of the bishop, Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte, who later became Pope [Julius III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Julius-III).

In 1547 Palestrina married Lucrezia Gori. Three sons were born to them: Rodolfo, Angelo, and Iginio. Only the last outlived his father. In 1551 Palestrina returned to Rome, where he assumed the first of his papal appointments, as musical director of the Julian Chapel choir, and thus was responsible for the music in [St. Peter’s](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saint-Peters-Basilica). Before he was 30 he published his first book of masses (1554), dedicated to Julius III, and the following year he was promoted to singer in the Pontifical Choir. About this time he became composer to the papal chapel. Palestrina repaid the pope’s patronage by composing a [mass](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) in his honour. Yet he did not neglect the [secular](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/secular) side of his art, for his first book of [madrigals](https://www.britannica.com/art/madrigal-vocal-music) (secular and spiritual part-songs) appeared in 1555, unfortunately at a time when the [lenient](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/lenient) regime of Julius III had given way to the sterner [discipline](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/discipline) of [Paul IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Paul-IV). A decree of the new pope forbade married men to serve in the papal choir, and Palestrina, together with two of his colleagues, received a small pension by way of compensation for their dismissal.

For the next five years Palestrina directed the choir of [St. John](https://www.britannica.com/place/St-Johns-Newfoundland-and-Labrador) Lateran, but his efforts were continually thwarted by singers whose quality was almost as limited as their number, which was restricted because very little money was available for music. Nevertheless, he gained admission for his eldest son, Rodolfo, then about 13, as a chorister. Eventually he broke away from this uncongenial [milieu](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/milieu). The chapter archives of St. John Lateran record that in July 1560 he and his son suddenly departed.

A year passed before Palestrina found employment. In March 1561 he accepted a new post at Santa Maria Maggiore. This post was more [congenial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/congenial) to him and he remained at it for about seven years. At the invitation of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este he then took charge of the music at the [Villa d’Este](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Villa-dEste) in Tivoli, a popular summer resort near Rome. He was in the cardinal’s service for four years, at which time he also worked as music master for a newly formed Seminarium Romanum (Roman Seminary), where his sons Rodolfo and Angelo became students.

Palestrina received an offer in 1568 to become musical director at the court of the emperor [Maximilian II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Maximilian-II-Holy-Roman-emperor) in Vienna. He refused the position because of the low salary and a disinclination to leave Rome. Palestrina’s terms were also too high when he was invited to the court at Mantua in 1583. The composer and the duke of Mantua, Guglielmo Gonzaga, an amateur musician of some pretensions, did become friends, however, and Palestrina was commissioned to write special [compositions](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/compositions) for the ducal chapel of Santa Barbara.

With the death in 1571 of the composer [Giovanni Animuccia](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Animuccia), musical director at the Vatican since 1555, there was a chance for Palestrina to return to his old post as musical director of the Julian choir. The chapter, eager to have him back, increased the salary, and he forthwith returned to St. Peter’s. When his growing fame as a composer prompted Santa Maria Maggiore to rehire him, St. Peter’s again raised his salary. In acknowledgment of his position as the most celebrated Roman musician, he was given in 1578 the title of master of music at the Vatican Basilica.

The series of [epidemics](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/epidemics) that swept through central [Italy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Italy) in the late 1570s carried off his wife and his two elder sons, both of whom showed great musical promise. He himself fell seriously ill. Grieving over his wife’s death, he announced his intention of becoming a priest, to the delight of the pope, [Gregory XIII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gregory-XIII). After having been made a canon, however, he renounced his vows in order to marry (1581) Virginia Dormoli, widow of a wealthy merchant. Although he spent considerable time administering her fortune, he retained his position at St. Peter’s and continued to compose.

Although an attempt in 1585 to make Palestrina musical director of the Pontifical Choir proved abortive, he was considered by all the popes under whom he served as the official composer for the choir, and it is recorded that he marched at the head of the pontifical singers on the occasion of erecting the great Egyptian obelisk in the piazza of St. Peter’s.

Pope Gregory XIII had [commissioned](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/commissioned) Palestrina and Annibale Zoilo to restore the plainchant, or [plainsong](https://www.britannica.com/art/plainsong-music) (a traditional liturgical chant sung in unison), then in use to a more authentic form. The task proved too great, and Palestrina’s editorial work gave way to a flow of creative music. Much of it was published during the last 12 years of his life, including volumes of motets (choral compositions based on sacred texts), masses, and madrigals. He also helped to found an association of professional musicians called the Vertuosa Compagnia dei Musici.

# Music of Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina

[Palestrina’s](https://www.britannica.com/place/Praeneste) musical output, though vast, maintained a remarkably high standard in both sacred and [secular](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/secular) works. His 105 [masses](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) embrace many different styles, and the number of voices used ranges from four to eight. The time-honoured technique of using a [cantus firmus](https://www.britannica.com/art/cantus-firmus) (preexistent [melody](https://www.britannica.com/art/melody) used in one voice part) as the tenor is found in such masses as _Ecce sacerdos magnus_; _[L’Homme armé](https://www.britannica.com/topic/LHomme-arme-mass-by-Palestrina)_; _Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la_; _Ave Maria_; _Tu es Petrus_; and _Veni Creator Spiritus_. These titles refer to the source of the particular cantus firmus. Palestrina’s mastery of [contrapuntal](https://www.britannica.com/art/counterpoint-music) ingenuity may be appreciated to the fullest extent in some of his canonic masses (in which one or more voice parts are derived from another voice part). His ability to ornament and decorate a solemn plainchant, making it an [integral](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/integral) part of the texture and sometimes almost indistinguishable from the other, freely composed parts, is evident from some of his masses based on [hymn](https://www.britannica.com/topic/hymn) melodies.

By far the greatest number of masses employ what has come to be known as the [parody](https://www.britannica.com/art/parody-music) technique, by which a composer made use either of his own [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) or that of others as a starting point for the new [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition). Many other masses derive from musical ideas by Palestrina’s predecessors or contemporaries. Yet another type of [mass](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) is demonstrated by the nine works written for Mantua; in these the Gloria and Credo sections are so arranged that plainsong and [polyphony](https://www.britannica.com/art/polyphony-music) alternate throughout. Finally, there is a small but important group of masses that are in free style, the musical material being entirely original. Perhaps the best known example is the _Missa brevis_ for four voices.

Palestrina’s [motets](https://www.britannica.com/art/motet), of which more than 250 are [extant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/extant), display almost as much variety of form and type as do his masses. Most of them are in some clearly defined form, occasionally reflecting the shape of the liturgical text, though comparatively few are based on plainsong. Many of them paraphrase the chant, however, with an artistry that is every bit as successful as that of the masses. On the same level as the canonic masses are such motets as _Cum ortus fuerit_ and _Accepit Jesus calicem_, the latter apparently a favourite of the composer’s—an assumption justified because he is depicted holding a copy of it in a portrait now in the Vatican.

His 29 motets based on texts from the [Song of Solomon](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Song-of-Solomon) afford numerous examples of “madrigalisms”: the use of suggestive musical phrases evoking picturesque features, apparent either to the ear or to the eye, sometimes to both. In the offertories, Palestrina completely abandons the old cantus firmus technique and writes music in free style, whereas in the hymns he paraphrases the traditional melody, usually in the highest voice. In the _Lamentations of Jeremiah_ he brings effective contrast to bear on the sections with Hebrew and Latin text, the former being melismatic (floridly vocalized) in style and the latter simpler and more solemn. His [Magnificats](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Magnificat) are mainly in four sets of eight, each set [comprising](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/comprising) a [Magnificat](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Magnificat) on one of the eight “tones”: _alternatim_ structure is used here as in the Mantua masses.

Although Palestrina’s madrigals are generally considered of less interest than his sacred music, they show as keen a sense for pictorial and pastoral elements as one finds in any of his contemporaries. Over and above this, he is to be remembered for his early exploitation of the narrative [sonnet](https://www.britannica.com/art/sonnet) in [madrigal](https://www.britannica.com/art/madrigal-vocal-music) form, notably in _Vestiva i colli_, which was frequently reprinted and imitated. His settings of Petrarch’s poems also are of an exceptionally high order.

At the end of the 19th century the view that Palestrina represented the loftiest peak of Italian polyphony was in some ways [detrimental](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/detrimental) to his reputation, for it cast his music into rigid preconceptions. Even more unfortunate was the insistence on “counterpoint in the style of Palestrina” in the examination requirements of academies and universities, for such requirements stultified a style that Palestrina had used with great flexibility. Generations of fledgling composers were taught to revere the music of Palestrina as a symbol of all that was pure in [ecclesiastical](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ecclesiastical)[counterpoint](https://www.britannica.com/art/counterpoint-music). Indeed, the greater part of his musical output, and in particular his masses (where his unerring sense of tonal architecture may be heard at its best), still remains worthy of admiration.

Palestrina, unlike [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johann-Sebastian-Bach), did not have to be rediscovered in the 19th century, though the dissemination of his achievement was helped by the interest of [Romantic](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/Romantic) composers. There always was a Palestrinian tradition, mainly because his music supplied the need for a well-regulated [formal system](https://www.britannica.com/topic/formal-system) to be used by the embryonic composer in presenting himself to the musical world. *   How did Palestrina's music influence later composers and church music?  

[Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina) was an Italian composer whose work had a significant influence on later composers and church music. His mastery of counterpoint and polyphony, especially evident in his masses and motets, established him as a model for [Renaissance](https://www.britannica.com/art/musical-composition/Development-of-composition-in-the-Middle-Ages#ref64574) sacred music.

Palestrina's style, marked by its purity and clarity, became a standard for [strict counterpoint](https://www.britannica.com/art/counterpoint-music/The-20th-century#ref64549) in academic settings, influencing generations of composers. His emphasis on the intelligibility of text in sacred music also had a lasting impact on the composition of church music, ensuring that the words were clearly understood amidst the intricate vocal lines.

**Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina** (born c. 1525, [Palestrina](https://www.britannica.com/place/Praeneste), near [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome) [Italy]—died February 2, 1594, Rome) was an Italian [Renaissance](https://www.britannica.com/event/Renaissance) composer of more than 105 masses and 250 motets, a master of contrapuntal [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition).

Palestrina lived during the period of the Roman Catholic [Counter-Reformation](https://www.britannica.com/event/Counter-Reformation) and was a primary representative of the 16th-century [conservative](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/conservative) approach to [church music](https://www.britannica.com/topic/liturgical-music).

## Life

Palestrina was born in a small town where his ancestors are thought to have lived for generations, but as a child he was taken to nearby Rome. In 1537 he was one of the choirboys at the basilica of [Santa Maria Maggiore](https://www.britannica.com/place/Santa-Maria-Maggiore-church-Rome-Italy), where he also studied [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) between 1537 and 1539. In 1544 Palestrina was engaged as organist and singer in the cathedral of his native town. His duties included playing the organ, helping with the choir, and teaching music. His pay was that of a [canon](https://www.britannica.com/art/canon-music) and would have been received in money and kind. His [prowess](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/prowess) at the church there attracted the attention of the bishop, Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte, who later became Pope [Julius III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Julius-III).

In 1547 Palestrina married Lucrezia Gori. Three sons were born to them: Rodolfo, Angelo, and Iginio. Only the last outlived his father. In 1551 Palestrina returned to Rome, where he assumed the first of his papal appointments, as musical director of the Julian Chapel choir, and thus was responsible for the music in [St. Peter’s](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saint-Peters-Basilica). Before he was 30 he published his first book of masses (1554), dedicated to Julius III, and the following year he was promoted to singer in the Pontifical Choir. About this time he became composer to the papal chapel. Palestrina repaid the pope’s patronage by composing a [mass](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) in his honour. Yet he did not neglect the [secular](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/secular) side of his art, for his first book of [madrigals](https://www.britannica.com/art/madrigal-vocal-music) (secular and spiritual part-songs) appeared in 1555, unfortunately at a time when the [lenient](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/lenient) regime of Julius III had given way to the sterner [discipline](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/discipline) of [Paul IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Paul-IV). A decree of the new pope forbade married men to serve in the papal choir, and Palestrina, together with two of his colleagues, received a small pension by way of compensation for their dismissal.

For the next five years Palestrina directed the choir of [St. John](https://www.britannica.com/place/St-Johns-Newfoundland-and-Labrador) Lateran, but his efforts were continually thwarted by singers whose quality was almost as limited as their number, which was restricted because very little money was available for music. Nevertheless, he gained admission for his eldest son, Rodolfo, then about 13, as a chorister. Eventually he broke away from this uncongenial [milieu](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/milieu). The chapter archives of St. John Lateran record that in July 1560 he and his son suddenly departed.

A year passed before Palestrina found employment. In March 1561 he accepted a new post at Santa Maria Maggiore. This post was more [congenial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/congenial) to him and he remained at it for about seven years. At the invitation of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este he then took charge of the music at the [Villa d’Este](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Villa-dEste) in Tivoli, a popular summer resort near Rome. He was in the cardinal’s service for four years, at which time he also worked as music master for a newly formed Seminarium Romanum (Roman Seminary), where his sons Rodolfo and Angelo became students.

Palestrina received an offer in 1568 to become musical director at the court of the emperor [Maximilian II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Maximilian-II-Holy-Roman-emperor) in Vienna. He refused the position because of the low salary and a disinclination to leave Rome. Palestrina’s terms were also too high when he was invited to the court at Mantua in 1583. The composer and the duke of Mantua, Guglielmo Gonzaga, an amateur musician of some pretensions, did become friends, however, and Palestrina was commissioned to write special [compositions](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/compositions) for the ducal chapel of Santa Barbara.

![Image 12: shohei ohtani, plants, andy wharhol art](https://cdn.britannica.com/marketing/inline-right.webp)

![Image 13: Mobile](https://cdn.britannica.com/marketing/inline-mobile.webp?w=400)

With the death in 1571 of the composer [Giovanni Animuccia](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Animuccia), musical director at the Vatican since 1555, there was a chance for Palestrina to return to his old post as musical director of the Julian choir. The chapter, eager to have him back, increased the salary, and he forthwith returned to St. Peter’s. When his growing fame as a composer prompted Santa Maria Maggiore to rehire him, St. Peter’s again raised his salary. In acknowledgment of his position as the most celebrated Roman musician, he was given in 1578 the title of master of music at the Vatican Basilica.

The series of [epidemics](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/epidemics) that swept through central [Italy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Italy) in the late 1570s carried off his wife and his two elder sons, both of whom showed great musical promise. He himself fell seriously ill. Grieving over his wife’s death, he announced his intention of becoming a priest, to the delight of the pope, [Gregory XIII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gregory-XIII). After having been made a canon, however, he renounced his vows in order to marry (1581) Virginia Dormoli, widow of a wealthy merchant. Although he spent considerable time administering her fortune, he retained his position at St. Peter’s and continued to compose.

Although an attempt in 1585 to make Palestrina musical director of the Pontifical Choir proved abortive, he was considered by all the popes under whom he served as the official composer for the choir, and it is recorded that he marched at the head of the pontifical singers on the occasion of erecting the great Egyptian obelisk in the piazza of St. Peter’s.

Pope Gregory XIII had [commissioned](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/commissioned) Palestrina and Annibale Zoilo to restore the plainchant, or [plainsong](https://www.britannica.com/art/plainsong-music) (a traditional liturgical chant sung in unison), then in use to a more authentic form. The task proved too great, and Palestrina’s editorial work gave way to a flow of creative music. Much of it was published during the last 12 years of his life, including volumes of motets (choral compositions based on sacred texts), masses, and madrigals. He also helped to found an association of professional musicians called the Vertuosa Compagnia dei Musici.

Born: c. 1525, Palestrina, near Rome [Italy]_(Show more)_

Died: February 2, 1594, Rome _(Show more)_

Notable Works: [“Accepit Jesus calicem”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Accepit-Jesus-calicem)[“Ave Maria”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ave-Maria-mass-by-Palestrina)[“Cum ortus fuerit”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Cum-ortus-fuerit)[“Ecce sacerdos magnus”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ecce-sacerdos-magnus)[“L’Homme armé”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/LHomme-arme-mass-by-Palestrina)[“Lamentations of Jeremiah”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lamentations-of-Jeremiah)[“Missa brevis”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Missa-brevis)[“Pope Marcellus Mass”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pope-Marcellus-Mass)[“Tu es Petrus”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Tu-es-Petrus)[“Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la)[“Veni Creator Spiritus”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Veni-Creator-Spiritus-mass-by-Palestrina)[“Vestiva i colli”](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Vestiva-i-colli)_(Show more)_

Two years before Palestrina’s death, the new pope, [Clement VIII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Clement-VIII-pope), increased his pension, and the same year, in a singular mark of respect and admiration, fellow composers paid their elderly senior the [compliment](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/compliment) of writing 16 settings of the Vesper Psalms to his praise. In return, Palestrina sent them a [motet](https://www.britannica.com/art/motet) on the appropriate text: _Vos amici mei estis_ “You are my friends, if you do what I teach, said the Lord.”

# Music of Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina

[Palestrina’s](https://www.britannica.com/place/Praeneste) musical output, though vast, maintained a remarkably high standard in both sacred and [secular](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/secular) works. His 105 [masses](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) embrace many different styles, and the number of voices used ranges from four to eight. The time-honoured technique of using a [cantus firmus](https://www.britannica.com/art/cantus-firmus) (preexistent [melody](https://www.britannica.com/art/melody) used in one voice part) as the tenor is found in such masses as _Ecce sacerdos magnus_; _[L’Homme armé](https://www.britannica.com/topic/LHomme-arme-mass-by-Palestrina)_; _Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la_; _Ave Maria_; _Tu es Petrus_; and _Veni Creator Spiritus_. These titles refer to the source of the particular cantus firmus. Palestrina’s mastery of [contrapuntal](https://www.britannica.com/art/counterpoint-music) ingenuity may be appreciated to the fullest extent in some of his canonic masses (in which one or more voice parts are derived from another voice part). His ability to ornament and decorate a solemn plainchant, making it an [integral](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/integral) part of the texture and sometimes almost indistinguishable from the other, freely composed parts, is evident from some of his masses based on [hymn](https://www.britannica.com/topic/hymn) melodies.

By far the greatest number of masses employ what has come to be known as the [parody](https://www.britannica.com/art/parody-music) technique, by which a composer made use either of his own [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music) or that of others as a starting point for the new [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition). Many other masses derive from musical ideas by Palestrina’s predecessors or contemporaries. Yet another type of [mass](https://www.britannica.com/art/mass-music) is demonstrated by the nine works written for Mantua; in these the Gloria and Credo sections are so arranged that plainsong and [polyphony](https://www.britannica.com/art/polyphony-music) alternate throughout. Finally, there is a small but important group of masses that are in free style, the musical material being entirely original. Perhaps the best known example is the _Missa brevis_ for four voices.

Palestrina’s [motets](https://www.britannica.com/art/motet), of which more than 250 are [extant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/extant), display almost as much variety of form and type as do his masses. Most of them are in some clearly defined form, occasionally reflecting the shape of the liturgical text, though comparatively few are based on plainsong. Many of them paraphrase the chant, however, with an artistry that is every bit as successful as that of the masses. On the same level as the canonic masses are such motets as _Cum ortus fuerit_ and _Accepit Jesus calicem_, the latter apparently a favourite of the composer’s—an assumption justified because he is depicted holding a copy of it in a portrait now in the Vatican.

His 29 motets based on texts from the [Song of Solomon](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Song-of-Solomon) afford numerous examples of “madrigalisms”: the use of suggestive musical phrases evoking picturesque features, apparent either to the ear or to the eye, sometimes to both. In the offertories, Palestrina completely abandons the old cantus firmus technique and writes music in free style, whereas in the hymns he paraphrases the traditional melody, usually in the highest voice. In the _Lamentations of Jeremiah_ he brings effective contrast to bear on the sections with Hebrew and Latin text, the former being melismatic (floridly vocalized) in style and the latter simpler and more solemn. His [Magnificats](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Magnificat) are mainly in four sets of eight, each set [comprising](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/comprising) a [Magnificat](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Magnificat) on one of the eight “tones”: _alternatim_ structure is used here as in the Mantua masses.

Although Palestrina’s madrigals are generally considered of less interest than his sacred music, they show as keen a sense for pictorial and pastoral elements as one finds in any of his contemporaries. Over and above this, he is to be remembered for his early exploitation of the narrative [sonnet](https://www.britannica.com/art/sonnet) in [madrigal](https://www.britannica.com/art/madrigal-vocal-music) form, notably in _Vestiva i colli_, which was frequently reprinted and imitated. His settings of Petrarch’s poems also are of an exceptionally high order.

At the end of the 19th century the view that Palestrina represented the loftiest peak of Italian polyphony was in some ways [detrimental](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/detrimental) to his reputation, for it cast his music into rigid preconceptions. Even more unfortunate was the insistence on “counterpoint in the style of Palestrina” in the examination requirements of academies and universities, for such requirements stultified a style that Palestrina had used with great flexibility. Generations of fledgling composers were taught to revere the music of Palestrina as a symbol of all that was pure in [ecclesiastical](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ecclesiastical)[counterpoint](https://www.britannica.com/art/counterpoint-music). Indeed, the greater part of his musical output, and in particular his masses (where his unerring sense of tonal architecture may be heard at its best), still remains worthy of admiration.

Palestrina, unlike [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Johann-Sebastian-Bach), did not have to be rediscovered in the 19th century, though the dissemination of his achievement was helped by the interest of [Romantic](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/Romantic) composers. There always was a Palestrinian tradition, mainly because his music supplied the need for a well-regulated [formal system](https://www.britannica.com/topic/formal-system) to be used by the embryonic composer in presenting himself to the musical world. # Research: Preset 08 — Suspension Garland (Role A: history and primary sources)

**Retrieval date:** 2026-07-15 (UTC)  
**Preset claim under review:** “prepared suspensions resolve across strong beats”; Fux/Palestrina reference; current Species IV baseline; transport required.

## Summary

The coherent intersection is narrow but real: Fux’s fourth species isolates a repeatable pedagogical chain—consonant preparation on the metrically weaker half, the same pitch sustained into a stronger position where another voice makes it dissonant, then downward stepwise consonant resolution—while Palestrina’s four-voice practice frequently uses accented, longer-note suspensions inside a much freer mixture of imitation, passing motion, changing voice counts, and cadential pacing. “Across strong beats” should therefore mean **a note begins consonantly before a metric accent, is retained across that accent as a controlled dissonance, and resolves after it (normally down by step)**, not “any long note crossing a barline,” not “all voices suspend,” and not “Palestrina wrote continuous fourth-species exercises.” [Fux/Mann, pp. 55–63](https://ia904500.us.archive.org/23/items/pdfy-_OKTX_2lKsXA_zvN/Counterpoint,%20Fux,%20by%20Alfred%20Mann_text.pdf) [Anders et al., paras. 17–22, Table 1](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/)

## 1. Scope and corpus

1. **Fux:** Johann Joseph Fux, *Gradus ad Parnassum* (Vienna, 1725), Part II dialogue between “Aloysius” (the idealized Palestrina teacher) and “Josephus.” The operative primary-source section is two-part fourth species, Mann translation pp. 55–63; the later multi-part “ligature” discussion begins p. 94. This is a graded exercise system, not a transcription of sixteenth-century composing practice. The 1725 Latin facsimile confirms title, date, and publication context. [1725 facsimile](http://tmg.huma-num.fr/xtf/view?docId=bookreader%2FFux_1725%2FFux_1725.xml) [Mann translation](https://ia904500.us.archive.org/23/items/pdfy-_OKTX_2lKsXA_zvN/Counterpoint,%20Fux,%20by%20Alfred%20Mann_text.pdf)
2. **Palestrina, selected score witnesses:** the four-voice motets *Sicut cervus* (first published 1587, *Motectorum liber secundus*, no. 10) and *Super flumina Babylonis* (CPDL catalogs four voices and first publication in the same 1587 book, no. 3). Modern CPDL transcriptions preserve four independent parts but may modernize clefs, barlines, pitch, or note values; claims tied to modern measure numbers are edition-specific. [*Sicut cervus* catalog/score witnesses](https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Sicut_cervus_%28Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina%29) [*Super flumina* catalog/score witnesses](http://cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Super_flumina_Babylonis_a_4_(Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina))
3. **Palestrina, corpus check:** Hanson's enumeration covers all 210 four-voice Ordinary movements in forty four-voice masses (18,313 modern-edition bars), using the Fratelli Scalera complete edition. Anders et al. use the first 36 Agnus movements in music21’s Palestrina corpus; that sample is explicitly arbitrary and all happen to be encoded in 4/2. These corpora are used to test whether “garlands” are representative, not to collapse all Palestrina into two motets. [Hanson](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina) [Anders et al., paras. 24–39](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/)
4. **Excluded scope:** no claim to copy a Palestrina melody; no claim that two late motets represent every mass, motet, madrigal, voice count, or career phase; no claim that Fux’s eighteenth-century rules are a documentary account of Palestrina’s workshop.

## 2. Historical and aesthetic context

- **Palestrina’s setting.** Palestrina (c. 1525–1594) worked chiefly in Roman sacred institutions: organist/singer at Palestrina, Julian Chapel director from 1551, then St John Lateran and Santa Maria Maggiore, returning to St Peter’s in 1571. His output spans over 105 masses and 250 motets and uses cantus-firmus, parody, canon, free composition, chant paraphrase, and differing voice counts. Suspension treatment belongs to a broad vocal contrapuntal language, not a standalone personal trademark. [Britannica, “Life” and “Music”](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina)
- **Counter-Reformation context, without the myth.** Concerns about sacred decorum and intelligible words formed part of Catholic reform, but the Council of Trent’s final action on music was limited and delegated details locally. The story that *Missa Papae Marcelli* single-handedly “saved polyphony” is a later legend, not a sound basis for the preset. [Monson, “The Council of Trent Revisited,” abstract](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2002.55.1.1)
- **Fux’s setting.** Fux (c. 1660–1741) was an Austrian Baroque court and church musician; *Gradus* appeared late in his career in 1725. It preserves and systematizes *stile antico* for training through deliberately abstract cantus-firmus tasks. The dialogue’s Palestrina persona signals aspiration and authority, not identity between the exercise and historical repertoire. [FUX online](https://fux-online.at/cms_seite.php?content=1&lang=E&menu=1) [Dodi, “preservation of stile antico”](https://periodicos.ufrn.br/artresearchjournal/article/download/31434/16949/110579)

## 3. Career/style evolution (only where defensible)

- **Palestrina:** early Roman advancement and first publications (mass book, 1554; madrigals, 1555) precede several institutional moves; from his 1571 return to St Peter’s through the 1580s–90s he published heavily across masses, motets, and madrigals. The selected 1587 motets are therefore mature/late-career sacred works, but their four-voice texture is only one part of a varied output. [Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina)
- **No defensible suspension “career arc.”** Hanson specifically looked for chronological patterns across the mass corpus and found none for the nine enumerated dissonance devices except a marked decline in *nota cambiata* usage. It would be unsupported to advertise mature Palestrina as “more suspension-heavy” or to turn this preset into a career-evolution narrative. [Hanson, discussion following Table 1](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina)
- **Fux:** the relevant evolution is reception and abstraction: a late-career 1725 pedagogy became enormously influential, while Fux’s own stylistically varied compositional career is outside this preset. Do not label the generated result “Fux’s compositional style.”

## 4. Persistent traits versus work-/system-specific traits

### Persistent or corpus-supported

- Suspensions are accented dissonances: in Anders et al.’s sample they cluster on strong beat 1 and strong beat 3, are approached by pitch repetition (a held/tied tone), and resolve by downward step; their dissonant portions are quarter or half notes in the encoding. The study found 265 beat-1 and 313 beat-3 cases, versus larger passing-tone categories on weak beats. [Anders et al., Table 1 and paras. 40–52](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/)
- In Hanson’s much larger four-voice mass corpus, 4–3 was the most frequent of the nine enumerated devices, averaging about once every four bars; 7–6 averaged about once every ten bars. The corpus also includes 9–8, 2–3, 2–1, double suspensions, and contextual exceptions. [Hanson, Table 1 and accompanying text](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina)
- The texture remains contrapuntal and mixed: weak-beat passing/neighbor motion coexists with stronger-beat suspensions. PeerJ’s notated primary example, *Missa De Beata Marie Virginis* II, Agnus, mm. 24–26, places passing tones, a neighbor tone, and a suspension in close proximity. [Anders et al., Fig. 1](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/#fig-1)

### Fux-/exercise-specific or selected-work-specific

- Continuous half-note-against-whole-note syncopation, a fixed cantus firmus, and maximizing a chain of ligatures are fourth-species constraints. They are useful for making the audible mechanism reliable, but they are not a statistical portrait of complete Palestrina movements.
- The two selected 1587 motets’ text-responsive imitation and phrase design should not be reduced to a suspension generator. Their edition histories also show transposition, changed note values, and added barlines in some modern scores. [CPDL *Sicut cervus* edition notes](https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Sicut_cervus_%28Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina%29)
- Cadential suspension density and exact interval species depend on bass/voice context. “Always 4–3” would exaggerate the most common type into the only type.

## 5. Relationship to peers and tradition

- Prepared dissonance, smooth stepwise vocal motion, imitation, modal organization, and cadential formulas were shared sixteenth-century contrapuntal vocabulary, not Palestrina’s private invention. Palestrina’s masses frequently reuse music by predecessors/contemporaries through parody technique; his motets and masses also draw on chant. [Britannica, “Music”](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina/Music)
- Lassus and Victoria belong to the same broad late-sixteenth-century sacred-polyphonic field, with locally and personally different practices. Hanson’s Palestrina-only counts justify a bounded Palestrina corpus claim, not uniqueness versus peers.
- Fux belongs to a later *stile antico* reception: he turns inherited polyphonic behavior into sequential species. The coherent reference is therefore **Palestrina corpus practice filtered through Fuxian pedagogy**, not a generic average of two coeval composers.

## 6. What “prepared suspensions across strong beats” honestly means

A qualifying event needs all four conditions:

1. **Preparation:** a voice attacks or is already sounding a pitch while that pitch forms a consonance with the controlling contrapuntal context.
2. **Retention across an accent:** the same pitch continues (tie/rearticulation equivalence in data may be necessary) while another voice changes, making the retained pitch dissonant on a metrically stronger position.
3. **Resolution:** the suspended voice then moves, normally **down by diatonic step**, into consonance.
4. **Metric hierarchy:** “strong” is relative. In a modern 4/2 representation, beat 1 is strongest and beat 3 is also strong; a suspension need not cross a modern barline. Renaissance source notation did not encode modern barlines, so transport should model pulse/accent, not fetishize UI barlines. [Anders et al., paras. 40–46 and Table 1](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/)

Thus the catalog wording is acceptable if read as **prepared notes retained into accents and resolved afterward**. It is misleading if read as “resolution occurs on the strong beat”: normally the *dissonant suspension* occupies the accent and resolution follows. It is also misleading if any held common tone is counted without testing preparation, dissonance, and resolution.

## 7. Documented intersection and excluded differences

### Intersection retained by the preset

- consonant preparation;
- sustained/repeated pitch into a metrically accented dissonance;
- controlled stepwise resolution, predominantly downward;
- chaining often enough to make syncopated tension/release audible;
- independent four-voice context rather than block-chord planing.

### Differences deliberately excluded

- **From Fux:** fixed two-note-against-one exercise rhythm, immutable cantus firmus, and near-continuous ligature chains are pedagogical restrictions, not requirements for historical Palestrina texture.
- **From Palestrina:** text setting, modal/ficta decisions, imitative points, cadential planning, variable rhythmic surface, voice-entry/withdrawal, sacred genre, and actual melodic material are not reproduced by “Species IV baseline.”
- **Historical gap:** Fux wrote roughly 130 years after Palestrina’s death. His Aloysius is an idealized authority; the preset must not claim direct reconstruction.

## 8. Common caricatures and myths to avoid

1. **“Palestrina saved polyphony at Trent.”** Unsupported legend; Trent did not simply ban polyphony and reverse itself after one mass. [Monson](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2002.55.1.1)
2. **“Fux equals Palestrina.”** Fux supplies a durable abstraction of *stile antico*, not a neutral empirical transcription.
3. **“Fourth species means every downbeat is dissonant.”** Consonant ligatures, breaks in species, cadential adjustments, and free counterpoint exist.
4. **“Suspension means any overlap.”** Without consonant preparation, accented dissonance, and controlled resolution, it is merely a held tone or another nonharmonic event.
5. **“Palestrina is uniformly smooth/pure.”** Corpus studies show varied dissonance categories, double suspensions, rare exceptions, and differing distributions; academic “purity” can rigidify a flexible style. [Hanson](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina) [Britannica, “Music”](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina/Music)
6. **“A garland is constant suspension saturation.”** Hanson’s averages support recurrent 4–3 and 7–6 motion, not one suspension in every voice on every accent.

## 9. Primary evidence and reference points

- **Fux, 1725 primary treatise:** original Latin title page/facsimile; Part II fourth species. [TMG/Bavarian State Library facsimile](http://tmg.huma-num.fr/xtf/view?docId=bookreader%2FFux_1725%2FFux_1725.xml)
- **Fux in translation:** Alfred Mann, *The Study of Counterpoint from Johann Joseph Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum*, pp. 55–63 (two-voice fourth species); p. 94ff. (multi-part ligature). [text PDF](https://ia904500.us.archive.org/23/items/pdfy-_OKTX_2lKsXA_zvN/Counterpoint,%20Fux,%20by%20Alfred%20Mann_text.pdf)
- **Palestrina score witness:** *Sicut cervus*, four voices, 1587, no. 10; CPDL supplies transcriptions including one based on *Opera omnia* V and explicitly reports which versions transpose/change note values. [CPDL](https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Sicut_cervus_%28Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina%29)
- **Palestrina score witness:** *Super flumina Babylonis*, four voices; CPDL score provenance includes transcriptions based on the 1875 Breitkopf & Härtel *Opera omnia* edition. [CPDL](http://cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Super_flumina_Babylonis_a_4_(Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina))
- **Exact musical locus:** *Missa De Beata Marie Virginis* II, Agnus, mm. 24–26 in the modern corpus edition: annotated passing tones, neighbor tone, and suspension. [Anders et al., Fig. 1](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/#fig-1)
- **Corpus counts:** Hanson, all 210 movements of forty four-voice masses, Tables 1–4; 4–3 first in rank and about one per four bars, 7–6 about one per ten; 104 suspensions resolve to a pitch already present in another voice; 193 of 4,681 counted 4–3s participate in double-suspension combinations. [Hanson](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina)

No melodic phrase is reproduced here.

## 10. Confidence, disagreements, and gaps

### Confidence by claim

- **High:** Fux fourth species codifies consonant preparation → accented retained dissonance → downward-step resolution; pp. 55–63.
- **High:** suspensions are frequent but mixed with other dissonance types in Palestrina; supported independently by a very large enumerated mass corpus and a smaller computational Agnus sample.
- **High:** 4–3 is substantially more common than 7–6 in Hanson’s four-voice corpus; “all types equal” would be false.
- **High:** the Trent “savior” story is a myth/overstatement.
- **Medium:** the two 1587 motets are suitable mature four-voice exemplars for source consultation; exact suspension locations were not asserted because accessible transcriptions differ in bars/note values and this run did not complete a note-by-note diplomatic comparison.
- **Medium:** a transport-aware Species IV generator can honestly evoke the intersection if UI copy says “inspired by prepared suspension practice,” not “authentic Palestrina.”

### Disagreements/qualification

- Hanson shows why textbook generalizations can fail: one cited manual calls 7–6 and 4–3 simply the most common suspended dissonances, but the corpus shows far more 4–3s; another calls 7–6/4–3 double suspension rare, while Hanson counts 111 in the four-voice masses. Corpus evidence should override tidy parity claims.
- CPDL’s *Super flumina* page gives “first published 1587,” while an edition note says its transcription derives through an 1875 edition from Gardano’s 1564 book of festal motets. Publication history therefore remains unresolved here; it does not affect the suspension claim but should be checked against RISM/original partbooks before final catalog metadata.
- Anders et al.’s algorithm intentionally misses complex cases and uses modern accent weights plus an arbitrary 36-Agnus sample. Its beat-1/beat-3 clusters corroborate, but do not replace, score reading or Hanson’s larger hand-enumerated corpus.

### Gaps / blocked or deferred work

- The Cambridge chapter on Fux’s theoretical precursors/successors was abstract-only/paywalled; skipped rather than paraphrased beyond available evidence.
- The Internet Archive restricted Jeppesen volume was not used as direct evidence; secondary summaries of Jeppesen were not promoted to primary evidence.
- Exact suspension-by-suspension measure lists for *Sicut cervus* and *Super flumina* require choosing one critical/diplomatic edition, then checking all four parts against the early print; modern CPDL measure numbers are not safely interchangeable.
- Hanson’s tables are image-based; the prose supplies key ratios and totals, but a reproducible dataset was not available in the article.
- No reliable evidence found for a chronological evolution of Palestrina’s suspension practice. Treat that as unknown, not absent.

## Sources

### Kept

- [Fux, *Gradus ad Parnassum* (1725) facsimile](http://tmg.huma-num.fr/xtf/view?docId=bookreader%2FFux_1725%2FFux_1725.xml) — primary treatise/date.
- [Fux/Mann, *The Study of Counterpoint*](https://ia904500.us.archive.org/23/items/pdfy-_OKTX_2lKsXA_zvN/Counterpoint,%20Fux,%20by%20Alfred%20Mann_text.pdf) — accessible faithful English translation and page references.
- [CPDL, *Sicut cervus*](https://www.cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Sicut_cervus_%28Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina%29) — score witnesses, provenance, publication and edition caveats.
- [CPDL, *Super flumina Babylonis*](http://cpdl.org/wiki/index.php/Super_flumina_Babylonis_a_4_(Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina)) — four-voice score witnesses and provenance.
- [Sandra Hanson, “Enumeration of Dissonance in the Masses of Palestrina”](https://symposium.music.org/volume-23/articles-1752877059/enumeration-of-dissonance-in-the-masses-of-palestrina) — large hand-enumerated four-voice corpus and warnings against textbook caricature.
- [Anders et al., “Machine learning…dissonance treatment in Palestrina”](https://peerj.com/articles/cs-244/) — transparent corpus method, exact notated locus, metric clusters, counts, and limitations.
- [Britannica, Palestrina](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Giovanni-Pierluigi-da-Palestrina) — vetted career/output overview and stylistic variety.
- [FUX online](https://fux-online.at/cms_seite.php?content=1&lang=E&menu=1) — Austrian Academy-associated Fux project for biography/reception context.
- [Craig Monson, “The Council of Trent Revisited”](https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2002.55.1.1) — document-based correction of the Trent myth.

### Dropped

- Wikipedia, generic counterpoint tutorials, Stack Exchange, Scribd study guides — redundant or non-authoritative where primary/scholarly sources were available.
- Restricted Jeppesen scans — inaccessible for direct verification.
- Cambridge *History of Western Music Theory* chapter — paywalled beyond abstract.
- SEO biographies and unsourced “Palestrina style” summaries — too general for measure/corpus claims.

## Preset-facing historical judgment

**Historically defensible bounded claim:** “A transport-synchronized fourth-species study inspired by Fux’s pedagogy and recurrent suspension practice in Palestrina’s four-voice sacred counterpoint: prepared held tones become accented dissonances and normally resolve downward by step.”

**Not defensible:** “An authentic Palestrina generator,” “the sound that saved church polyphony,” or “Palestrina’s style is continuous suspensions.”
